>> Hi everyone. I'm Alan. This is Patrick.
We are from Google DeepMind. And today
we wanted to talk to you about how to
build a trusted agent ecosystem.
>> [clears throat]
>> So, for the past year
we have noticed a lot of changes in the
industry. Everyone is building agents,
everyone is deploying agents, and there
has been a tremendous progress in making
agents smarter and faster, but the
industry still
needs to provide a clear answer for yet
another question, which is trust.
And
in order to make agents useful, you need
to give them data.
And [clears throat] to make them
especially useful, you need to give them
personal data. And when users give their
data to agents
they need guarantees that their data is
not going to just be shared across the
internet.
And right now users don't have a lot of
verifiable guarantees that they can rely
upon. They can ask the agent nicely to
please not share the data with everyone
else, but obviously this is not enough
to
uh protect the users.
And the reason for this is not only
because the agent is hard to control and
prevent these data leakages, but also
because the agents do not operate in a
vacuum. They are connected to the whole
ecosystem of different tools, models,
and agents.
And each component here can have a
challenge of its own. For example, when
you connect your agent to a third-party
MCP tool, you don't have any guarantees
that this tool is not just simply
leaking all of your data.
And in addition to this, this tool can
also attack the agent with a prompt
injection hidden in the tool
description. So, basically, your agent
is just trying to read the tool
description in the MCP server and it's
immediately attacked.
The second challenge is the model that
you need to use for model inference.
And most of the time you have to rely on
someone else to provide this model
inference servers. And technically, you
don't have verifiable guarantees that
this model providers are not just simply
logging all of your data and using it to
train the next generation of models. So,
you need to have guarantees when you
connect it to your agent.
And the situation is worsened
when you connect your agent to yet
another agent. And this agent can also
have the same exact problems as your
agent. So, they can transitively gossip
all of your data into the public web.
So, in order to build this trusted agent
ecosystem,
we need to answer the following
questions.
Uh we need to understand how we can
provide guarantees to the users so that
they they can trust agents. We need to
understand how can agents trust the
tools that they connected to them. And
how can agents trust each other?
And these are the kind of questions that
we're trying to answer in our project
Oak, which is a research project aimed
to make it possible for users to reason
about how their data is being processed
on the server side in a verifiable way.
And we use a set of technologies to
achieve this goal that we'll discuss in
a minute.
Okay, let's start with the most
important one here, which is
confidential computing.
Uh we all know how to protect user data
in transit with encrypted protocols and
how to protect user data at trust with
encrypted databases. But, when you're uh
processing user data in cloud, the data
still needs to be decrypted at some
point. And at this point, the cloud
provider will see all of the data inside
the VM.
And this is basically where the
confidential computing is trying to fill
this gap by providing protections for
data in use, meaning while the data is
being processed.
And the main idea of how it's doing this
is by creating so-called
trusted execution environments, which
you can think of as isolated encrypted
VMs that run on cloud,
and the key for encryption is hidden
inside the CPU as a hardware.
And when this VM is running,
the data is only being decrypted inside
the CPU,
processed inside the CPU, encrypted
back, and sent back to the memory. So,
the cloud provider cannot see what's
happening inside the VM, even though
they own the hardware.
An additional benefit that you get with
confidential computing is called the
remote attestation. And this is a
mechanism
that allows you to remotely verify what
is the code that's running on the server
side, which means what is the code
that's processing your data.
And this is done by the CPU, who
measures the VM. It checks what is the
binary that runs inside the VM, and
signs it with a key hidden in hardware.
So, that later you as a user can receive
a so-called attestation report, which
contains a signed hash of what's running
inside this VM.
One quick note when working with
confidential computing is you need to
understand the trust assumptions here,
because you trust the hardware
manufacturer to protect the key
correctly inside the CPU.
And also, users benefit from the split
trust between the cloud provider and the
hardware manufacturer.
Um
because the cloud provider has your data
but doesn't have the key, and hardware
manufacturer has the key but doesn't
have the data. So, if they want to steal
your data, these two big companies need
to collude together, which is a
significant reputational risk.
So, okay, we received the remote
attestation, but it only contains the
hash of the code. And obviously, it's
not enough for for us to reason what is
this code that's processing our data.
So, if you want to make remote
attestation meaningful, the code behind
it must be open source, so that auditors
can see that the code doesn't have
backdoors and it's processing the data

the code,
